results.name: digit_rule_size_principle
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on targets NOT matching that digit for sets of >=3 examples minus for 2-example sets; observed < null means people reject rule-violating targets more strongly as consistent examples accumulate (a size principle) than the model, whose mutual-similarity shortfall is identical for 2 or 4 uniform examples; observed > null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: digit_rule_size_principle
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one final digit, yes-rate on targets NOT matching that digit for sets of >=3 examples minus for 2-example sets; observed < null means people reject rule-violating targets more strongly as consistent examples accumulate (a size principle) than the model, whose mutual-similarity shortfall is identical for 2 or 4 uniform examples; observed > null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cats = pd.unique(sets)
    info = {}
    for s in cats:
        xs = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        u = len(xs) >= 2 and len({x % 10 for x in xs}) == 1
        info[s] = (len(xs) if u else 0, xs[0] % 10)
    sv = sets.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    n = np.array([info[s][0] for s in sv])
    d = np.array([info[s][1] for s in sv])
    nm = (t % 10) != d
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (n >= 3) & nm
    b = (n == 2) & nm
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: repdigit_concept_boost
results.description: In sets containing at least one repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on repdigit targets minus yes-rate on non-repdigit targets that share a final digit with some example (examples themselves excluded); observed > null means the model under-produces a "same-digit numbers" concept, observed < null that it over-credits it.
results.code:
# name: repdigit_concept_boost
# description: In sets containing at least one repdigit example (11,22,...,99), yes-rate on repdigit targets minus yes-rate on non-repdigit targets that share a final digit with some example (examples themselves excluded); observed > null means the model under-produces a "same-digit numbers" concept, observed < null that it over-credits it.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cats = pd.unique(sets)
    info = {}
    for s in cats:
        xs = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        info[s] = (any(x % 11 == 0 and 11 <= x <= 99 for x in xs), set(xs), {x % 10 for x in xs})
    sv = sets.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    has = np.array([info[s][0] for s in sv])
    is_ex = np.array([ti in info[s][1] for s, ti in zip(sv, t)])
    dm = np.array([(ti % 10) in info[s][2] for s, ti in zip(sv, t)])
    rep = (t % 11 == 0) & (t >= 11) & (t <= 99)
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = has & ~is_ex & rep
    b = has & ~is_ex & ~rep & dm
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: within_set_target_spread
results.description: Mean over sets with >=4 distinct targets (each with >=5 responses) of the standard deviation of per-target yes-rates within the set; observed > null means people discriminate among targets of the same set more sharply than the model predicts (model's target-level gradients too flat), observed < null the reverse.

results.name: even_odd_rule_asymmetry
results.description: Yes-rate on even targets in all-odd multi-example sets minus yes-rate on odd targets in all-even multi-example sets (targets sharing an example's final digit excluded); observed < null means people reject parity-violating targets more symmetrically for odd sets than the model's even-only privileged rule allows (an "odd numbers" rule is also used), observed > null means the even/odd asymmetry is even stronger than modelled.
results.code:
# name: even_odd_rule_asymmetry
# description: Yes-rate on even targets in all-odd multi-example sets minus yes-rate on odd targets in all-even multi-example sets (targets sharing an example's final digit excluded); observed < null means people reject parity-violating targets more symmetrically for odd sets than the model's even-only privileged rule allows (an "odd numbers" rule is also used), observed > null means the even/odd asymmetry is even stronger than modelled.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cats = pd.unique(sets)
    info = {}
    for s in cats:
        xs = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        par = 0 if all(x % 2 == 0 for x in xs) else (1 if all(x % 2 == 1 for x in xs) else -1)
        info[s] = (par if len(xs) >= 2 else -1, {x % 10 for x in xs})
    sv = sets.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    par = np.array([info[s][0] for s in sv])
    dm = np.array([(ti % 10) in info[s][1] for s, ti in zip(sv, t)])
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (par == 1) & (t % 2 == 0) & ~dm
    b = (par == 0) & (t % 2 == 1) & ~dm
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: prime_set_prime_target_boost
results.description: In multi-example sets whose examples are all primes, yes-rate on prime targets minus yes-rate on odd non-prime targets (targets equal to an example excluded); observed > null means the model under-produces a "prime numbers" concept, observed < null means it over-generalises to odd composites.

results.name: ordered_vs_unordered_examples
results.description: Among sets with >=3 examples, overall yes-rate on non-example targets for sets shown in monotonic (ascending or descending) order minus for sets shown in non-monotonic order; the model is order-invariant, so observed far from null means presentation order itself (a sequence-like display) changes how broadly people generalise (observed > null: ordered sets generalise more broadly than modelled).
results.code:
# name: ordered_vs_unordered_examples
# description: Among sets with >=3 examples, overall yes-rate on non-example targets for sets shown in monotonic (ascending or descending) order minus for sets shown in non-monotonic order; the model is order-invariant, so observed far from null means presentation order itself (a sequence-like display) changes how broadly people generalise (observed > null: ordered sets generalise more broadly than modelled).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str)
    cats = pd.unique(sets)
    info = {}
    for s in cats:
        xs = [int(x) for x in s.split(",")]
        if len(xs) < 3:
            info[s] = (-1, set(xs))
            continue
        dif = np.diff(xs)
        mono = bool(np.all(dif > 0) or np.all(dif < 0))
        info[s] = (1 if mono else 0, set(xs))
    sv = sets.values
    t = df["target"].astype(int).values
    k = np.array([info[s][0] for s in sv])
    is_ex = np.array([ti in info[s][1] for s, ti in zip(sv, t)])
    r = df["rating"].values.astype(float)
    a = (k == 1) & ~is_ex
    b = (k == 0) & ~is_ex
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: cross_position_digit_overlap
results.description: Among targets matching no example's final digit and whose decade lies outside the examples' decade range, yes-rate when a target digit appears in an example in the other position (target tens = an example's units, or target units = an example's tens) minus yes-rate otherwise; observed > null means people credit position-free digit identity (e.g. 31 vs 13) that the model, using only final digits and decade bands, misses.

results.name: unstructured_set_breadth
results.description: Yes-rate on targets sharing no final digit with any example in "unstructured" sets (>=3 examples, gcd 1, mixed parity, >=3 distinct final digits) minus the same rate in singleton sets; observed > null means people generalise more broadly from diverse, rule-less examples ("any number") than the model predicts, observed < null that they generalise less.
